title: Ocean Exploration
summary: One imagined expedition shows how ocean explorers combine maps, robots and carefully recorded samples.
paragraphs: A team heading for a remote underwater ridge faces a problem before anyone lowers a camera: it must decide where a dive is worth making. A chart derived from satellite measurements may suggest that a ridge is there, yet leave its smaller features unresolved. To narrow the search, the ship sends sound pulses towards the seabed and records the returning echoes across a wide strip. Repeated passes turn a rough outline into a map from which the team can plan routes. The new map still does not show what a camera would see on the bottom. Its first contribution is to make a large and uncertain search area more manageable.

The next stage trades wide coverage for close detail. A vehicle that carries a sonar near the bottom can distinguish features that blur together on a ship's map. But gaining detail has a cost: the narrow survey covers less ground on each pass, and planning it requires a reasonably good understanding of the terrain. The expedition assigns the close survey to strips where the first map suggests an abrupt change in slope. Several of those changes turn out to be smooth terraces. Others contain small ridges that are worth inspecting. The close survey is valuable partly because it removes attractive but unproductive targets from the dive plan.

The team uses two kinds of vehicles during the expedition. An untethered vehicle travels along a programmed route, collecting measurements over several hours before returning with its data. A remotely operated vehicle remains linked to the ship. Through the link, people at the surface can watch video and instruct the pilot to stop, turn or bring a sampler closer. In strong currents the tether can make manoeuvres more difficult, so the ship and vehicle must work together. The explorers use the untethered survey to find candidate sites and the linked vehicle to investigate selected details. Neither vehicle is expected to do the other's job equally well.

On one dive, the camera shows patches of pale material on several rocks. Appearance alone cannot establish whether the patches are living communities, mineral deposits or both. The pilot records the surrounding rock as well as the patch, and the team collects a nearby sample from a rock without a pale surface. A laboratory can compare the samples, but only if the expedition has kept their locations and collection conditions clear. The team therefore records a time and position with each sample number. A persuasive image may guide a question; the comparison and the records make it possible to examine an explanation after the ship returns.

Even an expedition with accurate positions can produce a distorted picture of the ridge. Cameras are deliberately aimed at places that look promising, so unusual structures and conspicuous animals can fill most of the footage. A viewer might conclude that those features are widespread, although the dives passed over ordinary ground without documenting much of it. To place the discoveries in context, the team also records video on preselected routes that cut across the ridge, including apparently unremarkable areas. These routes are less likely to yield dramatic images. Their value is that they give the researchers a basis for saying how often a feature appeared in the areas they sampled.

The expedition ends with a second task on shore: making its findings usable by someone who was not on the ship. A location labelled simply as a ridge summit is not enough. The team releases maps with notes about where the soundings were sparse, logs identifying the routes covered by each camera, and descriptions of how the samples were handled. A later expedition might use that record to revisit a site or to investigate a part of the ridge left in shadow. In this sense, an exploration is valuable not just for the places it makes visible, but for the uncertainties it gives the next team a practical way to investigate.

options: A closer survey that reduces the list of dive targets
Estimating the age of a ridge from its shape
Choosing complementary vehicles for different jobs
Checking how representative spectacular discoveries are
Turning a broad outline into a workable search area
Collecting comparisons that can be interpreted later
Replacing uncertain readings with better cameras

questions.quote: Its first contribution is to make a large and uncertain search area more manageable.
questions.explanation: The paragraph moves from a broad satellite outline to a ship survey that helps decide where to look.

questions.quote: The close survey is valuable partly because it removes attractive but unproductive targets from the dive plan.
questions.explanation: The closer map improves resolution and allows the team to rule out some possible dives. It does not estimate the ridge's age.

questions.quote: The explorers use the untethered survey to find candidate sites and the linked vehicle to investigate selected details.
questions.explanation: The paragraph contrasts the vehicle designs and explains how their roles complement each other.

questions.quote: the comparison and the records make it possible to examine an explanation after the ship returns
questions.explanation: The paired sample and collection records are what allow later analysis to distinguish competing explanations of an image.

questions.quote: Their value is that they give the researchers a basis for saying how often a feature appeared in the areas they sampled.
questions.explanation: The selected dive footage is potentially biased. Routes that cover ordinary terrain provide context for judging frequency.

questions.prompt: What does the ship's first survey allow the team to do?
options: Identify organisms from the echo of each patch.
Plan routes before examining the seabed in detail.
Predict the strength of currents at specific points.
Discard the need for further mapping.
questions.quote: Repeated passes turn a rough outline into a map from which the team can plan routes.
questions.explanation: The survey improves the map sufficiently to guide planning, while direct visual or fine-scale inspection comes later.

questions.prompt: Why does the team limit the more detailed survey to certain strips?
options: A detailed pass covers a narrower area.
The ship's map already identifies every small ridge.
Closer inspection works only on completely flat terrain.
The detailed instrument cannot operate near the bottom.
questions.quote: the narrow survey covers less ground on each pass
questions.explanation: Surveying at finer resolution makes coverage more expensive in time and routes, so the initial map guides where to focus.

questions.prompt: Which task most directly uses the link to the ship?
options: Storing measurements for later retrieval after a programmed survey.
Choosing where to send sound pulses from the ship.
Following a fixed route without surface instructions.
Changing a vehicle's movements while watching its video.
questions.quote: Through the link, people at the surface can watch video and instruct the pilot to stop, turn or bring a sampler closer.
questions.explanation: The link makes live observation and changes to the vehicle's actions possible.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of sampling a rock without a pale surface?
options: To test whether the camera can film at lower light levels.
To provide a comparison for the pale patch.
To replace the sample collected from the patch.
To establish how quickly the vehicle can finish a dive.
questions.quote: the team collects a nearby sample from a rock without a pale surface
questions.explanation: A nearby uncoated rock provides a point of comparison for analysing the material on the pale surface.

questions.prompt: What mistaken impression might arise from viewing only footage of promising locations?
options: Ordinary areas have never been crossed by a vehicle.
Every visible structure is an example of a mineral deposit.
Unusual features occupy more of the ridge than they actually do.
The expedition had no position records for its surveys.
questions.quote: A viewer might conclude that those features are widespread, although the dives passed over ordinary ground without documenting much of it.
questions.explanation: Selective filming can make striking discoveries seem more common than they are.

questions.prompt: Why does the expedition indicate where soundings were sparse?
options: To tell the next team where the map leaves greater uncertainty.
To guarantee that the unmeasured areas contain unusual animals.
To prevent future teams from revisiting mapped sites.
To show that the samples were all collected from a summit.
questions.quote: The team releases maps with notes about where the soundings were sparse
questions.explanation: Notes about coverage show where the map offers less information and where additional investigation could be useful.

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the author's overall view of ocean exploration?
options: A successful exploration eliminates any uncertainty about the seafloor.
Collecting samples is more valuable than choosing what to map.
Improving camera resolution is the main measure of progress.
Complementary observations and transparent records help others investigate what remains uncertain.
questions.quote: the uncertainties it gives the next team a practical way to investigate
questions.explanation: Across the article, different instruments and sampling methods address different limits. Recording those limits makes later work possible.
